title: Samples and populations
objectives: Tell a statistic from the parameter it estimates.
Tell an estimator, a rule, from an estimate, the number it gives.

screens.title: Draw a sample
screens.prose: A stock traded on 100 days. Each cell hides one day's return, in %. You cannot afford to look at all 100. You may look at 10.

params.colLabel: 100 trading days, one cell each (daily return, %)

state.caption: Tap a cell to reveal that day's return

screens.question: Tap any 10 days to see their returns.

hints.text: Any 10 cells will do. Try to spread them out.

feedback.correct: You have looked at 10 of the 100 days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap exactly 10 cells.

byKey.too-few: You have revealed fewer than 10 days. Tap a few more.
byKey.too-many: You have revealed more than 10 days. Tap one again to hide it.

explain.text: Your 10 days are a **sample**. All 100 days together are the **population**. Different taps would have shown you different returns.

canvas.caption: Your 10 days: a sample of the 100

screens.title: One sample, one average
screens.prose: A colleague picked 10 days at random. Their returns are now showing. The other 90 stay hidden.

params.colLabel: 100 trading days, one cell each (daily return, %)

state.caption: Sample A: 10 days picked at random

screens.question: What is the average return of the 10 shaded days?

widget.label: Average of sample A, in %
widget.accept: 0.42%: the ten returns add to 4.2%, and $4.2 / 10 = 0.42$.

hints.text: Add the ten shaded returns, then divide by how many there are.
Three days lost money: −0.3, −1.0 and −1.9. The other seven add to 7.4.

feedback.correct: The ten returns add to 4.2%, so the average is 0.42%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the ten shaded returns with their signs, then divide by 10.

byKey.sum: 4.2% is the total of the ten days. Divide by 10 to get the average.
byKey.dropped-minus: You added every return as if it were positive. Three of the days lost money: −0.3, −1.0 and −1.9.
byKey.per-hundred: You divided by 100, the size of the population. The sample has 10 days.

explain.text: The ten returns add to 4.2%, so their average is $\bar x = 0.42\%$. That number comes from 10 days only. The average of all 100 is still hidden.

screens.title: Parameter or statistic
screens.prose: Here are all 100 days. A number that describes the whole population is a **parameter**, such as its mean $\mu = 0.10\%$. A number computed from a sample is a **statistic**, such as sample A's $\bar x = 0.42\%$.

params.colLabel: 100 trading days, one cell each (daily return, %)

screens.question: Sort each number into parameter or statistic.

tokens.text: $p = 0.47$, the share of all 100 days that were up
$\bar x = 0.42\%$, the mean of sample A
$\hat p = 0.7$, the share of sample A that was up

hints.text: Ask of each number: was it computed from all 100 days, or from 10 of them?
Three numbers mention all 100 days. Three mention sample A.
$\mu$, $\sigma$ and $p$ describe all 100 days: parameters. $\bar x$, $s$ and $\hat p$ come from sample A: statistics.

feedback.correct: Greek letters for the population, Latin letters and hats for the sample.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A parameter uses every day in the population; a statistic uses only the sample.

byKey.mu: $\mu$ averages all 100 days, so it describes the population. It is a parameter.
byKey.sigma: $\sigma$ is the spread of all 100 days. It is a parameter.
byKey.p: $p$ counts up days among all 100. It is a parameter.
byKey.xbar: $\bar x$ uses only the 10 days of sample A. It is a statistic.
byKey.s: $s$ is the spread of the 10 days in sample A. It is a statistic.
byKey.phat: $\hat p$ is the share of up days in sample A only. It is a statistic.

explain.text: Each parameter has a statistic that estimates it: $\bar x$ for $\mu$, $s$ for $\sigma$, $\hat p$ for $p$. In practice the parameter is hidden. Sample A gave 0.42% where the truth is 0.10%.

screens.title: A second sample
screens.prose: A second colleague picks 10 days at random, sample B. Their average is $\bar x = -0.15\%$. Sample A gave 0.42%.

params.colLabel: 100 trading days, one cell each (daily return, %)

state.caption: Sample A: 0.42%. Sample B: −0.15%. One day is in both.

screens.question: Which number changed between the two samples?

options.text: The statistic $\bar x$ changed; the parameter $\mu$ did not
Both $\bar x$ and $\mu$ changed
options.why: You let the new sample move $\mu$. It is the mean of all 100 days, and no draw changes those days.

options.text: $\mu$ is now the average of the two samples, 0.135%
options.why: You pooled the two samples. Averaging 20 days gives another statistic, not the mean of all 100.

options.text: Neither: one of the colleagues made a mistake
options.why: You expected every sample to give the same answer. Both added correctly; they drew different days.

hints.text: Which number belongs to the 100 days, and which to the 10 that were drawn?
The population did not change between the two draws.
A new sample means new days, so a new $\bar x$. The 100 days, and so $\mu$, are the same.

feedback.correct: A statistic moves with the sample; the parameter stays put.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which number depends on the days drawn.

byKey.both: You let the new sample move $\mu$. It is the mean of all 100 days, and no draw changes those days.

explain.text: Sample A and sample B came from the same 100 days, yet gave 0.42% and −0.15%. The truth, $\mu = 0.10\%$, sat between them both times. A statistic is a moving target; the parameter is fixed but unknown.

canvas.caption: Same population, two samples, two different $\bar x$

screens.title: A rule and a number
screens.prose: The rule "add the 10 returns and divide by 10" is an **estimator**: $$\hat\mu = \bar X = \frac{1}{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10} X_i.$$ Its value on one sample is an **estimate**. On sample A the estimate is 0.42%. The hat says "an estimate of".

params.colLabel: 100 trading days, one cell each (daily return, %)

screens.question: Before anyone draws a sample, which of these is a random variable?

options.text: The estimator $\bar X$
The estimate 0.42%
options.why: You picked a number that is already known. 0.42% is what the rule gave for sample A; it cannot change.

options.text: The mean $\mu$
options.why: You treated the unknown as random. $\mu$ is fixed by the 100 days; we just cannot see it.

options.text: The sd $\sigma$
options.why: $\sigma$ is fixed by the 100 days, like $\mu$. Only the sample, and what we compute from it, is random.

hints.text: Which of these would come out differently if a different 10 days were drawn?
A capital letter marks a random variable.
Before the draw, the 10 returns $X_1, \dots, X_{10}$ are random, so their average $\bar X$ is random too.

feedback.correct: The estimator is random until the draw; then it lands on one estimate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what changes from one draw to the next.

byKey.mu: You treated the unknown as random. $\mu$ is fixed by the 100 days; we just cannot see it.

explain.text: Before the draw, $\bar X$ could be 0.42%, −0.15% or many other values. After it, we write the estimate in lower case, $\bar x = 0.42\%$. Capitals for the rule, lower case for the number it gave.

canvas.caption: $\bar X$ is the rule; $\bar x = 0.42\%$ and $\bar x = -0.15\%$ are two estimates

screens.title: Looking at every day
screens.prose: The risk team has more time. They record all 100 days and average them.

params.colLabel: 100 trading days, one cell each (daily return, %)

screens.question: What is the sampling error $\bar x - \mu$ now?

widget.label: Sampling error, in %
widget.accept: 0 exactly: a census averages the population itself, so $\bar x = \mu$.

hints.text: If the sample is every day, how does its average compare with $\mu$?
Every cell is shaded: the sample and the population are the same 100 days.
The average of all 100 days is $\mu$ by definition, so $\bar x - \mu = 0$.

feedback.correct: A census has no sampling error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The team averaged every day in the population.

byKey.sample-a: 0.32% was sample A's error, $0.42 - 0.10$. The team used all 100 days, not 10.
byKey.mu: 0.10% is $\mu$ itself. The error is the gap between $\bar x$ and $\mu$.

explain.text: When the sample is the whole population, the statistic is the parameter: $\bar x = \mu = 0.10\%$. That is a census, the edge case with no sampling error. Every real sample sits between: some days seen, some not.

screens.title: The manager's claim
screens.prose: A fund manager shows sample A. "Over 10 random days we averaged 0.42%. So our true mean daily return is 0.42%."

params.colLabel: 100 trading days, one cell each (daily return, %)

screens.question: What is wrong with the claim?

options.text: Nothing: the average of the data is the true mean
options.why: You treated the sample mean as $\mu$. Samples A and B came from the same days and gave 0.42% and −0.15%.

options.text: 0.42% is a statistic from 10 days; the true mean is unknown and could be quite different
The true mean must be below 0.42%, because a sample mean always overstates it
options.why: You gave the sample mean a built-in tilt. Sample B came in below $\mu$, so misses go both ways.

options.text: Ten days pins the true mean down to within 0.01%
options.why: You trusted 10 days too far. The two samples here differ by 0.57%.

hints.text: Is 0.42% computed from the population or from a sample?
Compare the two samples we drew from these same days.
Sample A gave 0.42% and sample B gave −0.15%. Neither is $\mu$; each is a statistic.

feedback.correct: The claim swaps a statistic for the parameter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what a different 10 days would have shown.

byKey.same: You treated the sample mean as the true mean. Samples A and B came from the same days and gave 0.42% and −0.15%.

explain.text: The manager wrote $\mu$ where only $\bar x$ was known. Here we can check: the true mean is 0.10%, a third of the claim. The honest sentence is "our estimate is 0.42%", with a word on how far off it might be.

screens.title: Hats on estimates
screens.prose:
Every time, a hidden parameter had a statistic standing in for it. We write a parameter as $\theta$ and its estimator as $\hat\theta$:
- the mean $\mu$, estimated by $\hat\mu = \bar x$
- the sd $\sigma$, estimated by $\hat\sigma = s$
- the proportion $p$, estimated by $\hat p$

A census is the one case where $\hat\theta = \theta$ for sure.
screens.question: A bank estimates the default rate $p$ of all its 20,000 loans from a random 400. In the bank's files, 12 of the 400 defaulted. How do we write the bank's number?

options.why: You wrote the parameter. 0.03 comes from 400 loans, so it is an estimate of $p$, written $\hat p$.

options.text: $\bar x = 12$
options.why: You reported the count of defaults. The estimate of a rate is the share, $12 / 400$.
$\theta$ stands for the unknown parameter itself. The hat marks the estimate.

hints.text: Is 0.03 computed from all 20,000 loans or from 400 of them?
$12 / 400 = 0.03$ comes from a sample, so it wears a hat: $\hat p = 0.03$.

feedback.correct: A statistic from 400 loans estimates the rate on all 20,000.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide first whether 0.03 describes the sample or the whole book.

explain.text: The share of defaults among the 400 is $12 / 400 = 0.03$, a statistic. It estimates $p$, the share among all 20,000, which nobody has counted. So we write $\hat p = 0.03$.

screens.title: A strategy's hit rate
screens.prose: A new strategy has made 50 trades: 29 winners and 21 losers. Its true hit rate $p$ is the share of winners over all the trades it would ever make.
screens.question: What is $\hat p$, the estimate of the hit rate?

hints.text: What share of the 50 trades won?
The winners bar is the count you need.

feedback.correct: $\hat p = 29 / 50 = 0.58$: an estimate, not the true rate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the winners by all 50 trades.

byKey.count: 29 is the number of winners. The hit rate is a share: divide by 50.
byKey.odds: You divided winners by losers, $29 / 21$. That is the odds, not the share of trades that won.
byKey.losers: 0.42 is the share that lost. The hit rate counts winners.

explain.text: $\hat p = 29 / 50 = 0.58$ is a statistic from 50 trades. The true $p$ could be 0.5 and the strategy lucky, or 0.65 and unlucky. Lesson 2 measures how far 50 trades can mislead.

screens.title: Statistics on the desk
screens.prose: Three numbers from a morning meeting.

rows: Fund X, its 252 daily returns last year
A poll of 1,000 voters on a trade deal
Fund X, its long-run daily volatility

screens.question: Select all that apply: which of these are statistics?

options.text: The sd of 1.1% from last year's 252 returns
The 54% from the poll of 1,000 voters
Fund X's long-run daily volatility $\sigma$
options.why: You counted the target as a statistic. $\sigma$ describes every day the fund could trade, so it is a parameter.

options.text: The share of all voters in favour, $p$
options.why: You counted the whole country's share. That is the parameter the poll estimates.

hints.text: Which numbers were computed from data someone actually has?
Two rows say "unknown". Those are what the other two estimate.
One year of returns and 1,000 voters are samples, so their numbers are statistics.

feedback.correct: One year of returns and one poll are samples; the long-run volatility and the national share are parameters.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A statistic is computed from a sample in hand.

byKey.sigma: You counted the target as a statistic. $\sigma$ describes every day the fund could trade, so it is a parameter.

explain.text: Last year's sd, $s = 1.1\%$, estimates the fund's volatility $\sigma$. The poll's $\hat p = 0.54$ estimates the national share $p$. Next year will give a different $s$, and a new poll a different $\hat p$.

ideas: A **parameter** describes the whole population: $\mu$, $\sigma$, $p$. It is fixed but usually unknown.
A **statistic** is computed from a sample: $\bar x$, $s$, $\hat p$. A new sample gives a new value.
An **estimator** $\hat\theta$ is a rule; an **estimate** is the number it gives on one sample. Only a census gives $\hat\theta = \theta$ for sure.

formula.name: The sample mean as an estimator
formula.note: Capital $X_i$ before the draw, lower-case $x_i$ and $\bar x$ after it.

summary.trap: A sample mean of 0.42% does not mean the true mean is 0.42%. Samples A and B gave 0.42% and −0.15% from the same 100 days.

quiz.prose: A poll of 800 voters finds that 46% back a plan.
quiz.question: What is 0.46?

options.text: An estimate $\hat p$ of the share of all voters who back the plan
The share $p$ of all voters who back the plan
options.why: You took the poll for the whole electorate. 0.46 comes from 800 people, so it estimates $p$.

options.text: The estimator: the rule for turning a poll into a share
options.why: The estimator is the rule, "count backers and divide by 800". 0.46 is the number it gave this time.

feedback.correct: A number from 800 voters estimates the share among all of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether 0.46 came from everyone or from a sample.

explain.text: 0.46 is a statistic, $\hat p = 0.46$, computed from 800 voters. The parameter $p$ is the share among every voter, which nobody has measured. Another poll of 800 would give a different $\hat p$.

quiz.prose: An index holds exactly 500 stocks. An analyst averages the dividend yield of all 500.
quiz.question: How far can her average be from the index's true mean yield because of sampling?

options.text: Not at all: she used the whole population
A little, because 500 is a finite sample
options.why: You treated the 500 as a sample. They are every stock in the index, so this is a census.

options.text: We cannot say without the standard deviation
options.why: With every stock included there is nothing left unseen, so the spread does not matter.

feedback.correct: A census has no sampling error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Did she leave any stock of the index out?

explain.text: The population is the 500 stocks, and she used all of them. Her average is the parameter itself. Errors in the data could still creep in, but not sampling error.

quiz.prose: You draw 10 days of a stock's returns at random and get $\bar x = 0.20\%$. A colleague draws 10 days from the same history.
quiz.question: What do you expect?

options.text: Her $\bar x$ will probably differ from 0.20%, and $\mu$ is the same for both of you
Her $\bar x$ will be 0.20% too, since it is the same stock
options.why: You expected the sample mean to be a fixed property of the stock. It depends on which days are drawn.

options.text: Her $\bar x$ will differ, and so will $\mu$
options.why: You let the draw move the parameter. $\mu$ belongs to the full history, which is the same for both of you.

options.text: Her $\bar x$ will be closer to $\mu$ than yours, since she drew second
options.why: The order of drawing gives no advantage. Each sample of 10 is as good as the other.

feedback.correct: Statistics vary from sample to sample; the parameter stays fixed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate what depends on the draw from what does not.

explain.text: Two samples of 10 days give two different $\bar x$, just as samples A and B did. Both estimate the same $\mu$. Which one lands closer is luck.

quiz.prose: A desk writes $\hat\sigma = 1.3\%$ in its daily risk report.
quiz.question: What does the hat tell you?

options.text: 1.3% is an estimate of $\sigma$, computed from a sample
1.3% is the true volatility, rounded
options.why: You read the hat as rounding. It marks an estimate, which can miss by more than rounding.

options.text: 1.3% is the largest the volatility can be
options.why: You read the hat as a ceiling. It only says the number estimates $\sigma$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what $\hat p$ and $\hat\mu$ meant.

explain.text: $\hat\sigma$ reads "sigma hat": an estimate of the volatility $\sigma$. The desk computed it from recent returns, a sample. The true $\sigma$ stays unknown.
